sources.text: The ruling, which could affect similar laws in other British Commonwealth countries, has spotlighted a legal system still intertwined with a former colonial power.

sources.headline: UK Privy Council overrules Trinidad and Tobago gay sex law
sources.text:
A man from Trinidad and Tobago has won a legal appeal lasting almost a decade in the last court of appeal available to him — the judicial committee of the Privy Council in former colonial power Britain.
Jason Jones, a gay man born in Trinidad and Tobago, had challenged the Caribbean nation's Sexual Offences Act outlawing consensusal sex between adult males, saying that it breached his fundamental rights under the country's constitution.
He initially won his case at Trinidad and Tobago's High Court, but the government and religious organizations managed to partially overturn the ruling once more, prompting Jones to the take the case to the island nation's highest appellate authority — the Privy Council in the UK.
"To discriminate against somebody simply because of who they choose to love is simply ridiculous," Jones told the Associated Press after Tuesday's judgment was rendered.
The Privy Council in London is the final court of appeal for some Commonwealth countries including Trinidad and Tobago, although that issue was already contentious in some circles prior to Tuesday's ruling. The Judicial Committee of the Privy Council is the final court of appeal for UK overseas territories, Crown dependencies and some Commonwealth countries, including Trinidad and TobagoImage: Photoshot/picture alliance
What did the London court rule?
A panel of five judges unanimously allowed Jones' appeal, dismissing a counter-appeal from the Caribbean country's Attorney General.
It found that two sections of the country's Sexual Offenses Act 1986, criminalizing "buggery" and "serious indecency" respectively among same-sex couples, violated Jones' fundamental rights to private and family life set out in the 1976 constitution.
The court wrote in its ruling that "the rights and interests of Mr Jones which are at stake involve a particularly important facet of his existence and identity since the ability to form an intimate and loving relationship with another person lies at the core of the right to private and family life."
The anti-gay laws that call for up to five years in prison have not been enforced in recent history, but critics say they still send an intimidating message.
Judge Philip Sales said as he announced the ruling that "the current understanding of the fundamental individual right to respect for private and family life is that it protects such a core part of human identity as one's sexual orientation."
Sales added that "laws which seek to criminalize such activities cannot be justified."
Trinidadian authorities argued that because the 1986 laws were passed with a super-majority and constituted criminal penalties that dated back to colonial times, prior to the constitution, they could be considered "existing law" and override the individual constitutional rights in certain circumstances.
But the Privy Council judges found that the so-called "proviso" for this special status — "unless the Act is shown not to be reasonably justifiable in a society that has proper respect for the rights and freedoms of the individual" — had not been met.
One of Jones' lawyers, Anand Ramlogan, is a former attorney general of Trinidad and Tobago and argued against this position earlier in the case.
"Constitutional rights exist precisely because majorities are not always right," Ramlogan said. "They ensure that the dignity and equality of every citizen are not left to the changing tides of public opinion." Who is the appellant?
Jason Jones is a 61-year-old born in Trinidad and Tobago.
Openly gay since the age of 16, he said he fled the country in 1996 because of homophobic violence and discrimination.
Speaking to the Associated Press on Tuesday after what he termed a "stunning victory," he said he would describe himself as a "very angry gay man," whose anger had helped him persist in his legal appeal for so many years.
"Society has treated me worse than a criminal," he said. "There is a real sense of vindication with this judgment. Finally, the courts are seeing that they need to step up because our politicians are so toothless."
He said he became inspired to speak out after losing friends to HIV/AIDS and after meeting American singer-songwriter Nina Simone when she toured the island nation for three weeks in 1984, when he was 19.
"Nina was the one who said, 'Jason, get off this rock and go see the world,'" he said, calling it a defining and life-changing experience.

Trinidad and Tobago may not enforce its 'buggery' law, but it carries a custodial sentence
Trinidad and Tobago's government, the country's Council of Evangelical Churches and its largest Hindu organization, Sanatan Dharm Maha Sabha, contested the case, which has wound its way through several courts since the appeal was launched in 2017.
In 2018, Trinidad's High Court found the laws unconstitutional. But in 2025, a local appeals court partially reversed the ruling. Trinidad's Court of Appeals subsequently allowed Jones to seek a ruling from the final appeals court in England.
The case was being closely watched by activists across the Caribbean, with similar laws in place in several other countries in the region.
The Bahamas decriminalized homosexuality in 1991.
The UK repealed laws in overseas territories Anguilla, the British Virgin Islands, the Cayman Islands, Montserrat and the Turks and Caicos Islands in 2001.
Judges in Barbados, Dominica, St. Lucia and Antigua and Barbuda have also recently struck down similar laws.
But in former British colonies Grenada, Jamaica, Trinidad and Tobago and St. Vincent and the Grenadines it remains a crime.
The UK only decriminalized gay sex in 1967, more than four centuries after the so-called "buggery" laws were first introduced under King Henry VII, and more than a century after the last executions for the crime. People still faced prosecution or the threat of it for consensual adult gay sex until after World War II, with surely the most famous later-years case being that of computing and codebreaking pioneer and war hero Alan Turing.

sources.headline: Trinidad and Tobago highest court overturns gay sex ban
sources.text:
Published on
11 November 2026 - 17:27 GMT+1
A decade-long legal battle led by LGBT+ Trinidadian activists successfully ended as Trinidad and Tobago's highest court overturned a long-running law criminalising gay sex.
The UK-based final court of appeal for British dependencies and overseas territories issued a unanimous decision Tuesday that the 1986 Sexual Offences Act could not be used to prosecute private, consensual sexual relations between adults of the same sex.
Seen as a landmark ruling for LGBT+ rights in the Caribbean, this law had previously carried sentences of two years for "serious indecency" and five years for "buggery".
"What I'm going to be doing in the coming months is very targeted activism about how the Caribbean, not just Trinidad and Tobago, deals with endemic homophobia," said LGBT+ Trinidadian activist Jason Jones after the verdict was read.
'Phenomenal victory for gay rights'
Freedom Law Chambers, the law firm that represented Jones, said in a statement that the judgement represented a "phenomenal victory for gay rights, equal dignity and respect for private and family life in Trinidad and Tobago."
The Judicial Committee of the Privy Council, which issued the decision, said constitutional rights must be interpreted in a way that makes them "practical and effective in the present day, not in the past."
The judgement was welcomed by UN Human Rights chief Volker Turk, who called it a significant milestone for rights and equality.
"I hope the judgment will help remove a longstanding source of stigma, exclusion, barriers and violence experienced by Trinidadians and Tobagonians based on sexual orientation and gender identity," Turk said.

sources.headline: Anti-homosexuality laws in Trinidad and Tobago overturned
sources.text: A UK court has overturned laws criminalising same-sex intimacy in Trinidad and Tobago.London's Judicial Committee of the Privy Council (JCPC), the Caribbean island's final court of appeal, ruled the laws were not in keeping with the "fundamental individual right to respect for private and family life."The judgement is the result of an 11-year legal battle brought by dual-citizen Jason Jones, 62, who said he hoped it would "accelerate the fight for full equality."Jones had successfully challenged the laws in 2018 in Trinidad's High Court, however the ruling was overturned on appeal by the Trinidadian government.It is the first time the JCPC has ever decided on a case to decriminalise same-sex intimacy, and campaigners hope it will spark similar successful legal challenges elsewhere in the Commonwealth.Prior to this historic decision, Trinidad and Tobago was one of some 34 Commonwealth countries continuing to criminalise homosexuality based on colonial-era British laws. Under these laws, consensual same-sex intimacy is punishable by imprisonment, and in some cases carries the death penalty.The Attorney General of Trinidad and Tobago had argued that the law was protected from legal challenges by the "savings law clauses" - which carried over existing British laws into newly independent states.Representatives for Jones argued that the laws violated an individual's right to privacy and argued the government's changes to the laws in 1986 - which saw stricter punishments introduced - meant the savings clause protections no longer applied.The judicial committee unanimously found in favour of Jones.Handing down the judgement, Lord Sales told the court the laws "cannot be regarded as reasonably justifiable in a society that has a proper respect for the rights and freedoms of an individual".Jones, human rights campaigner and appellant in the appeal, said: "These laws never reflected who we are as a people and a nation - diverse, multiracial, and secular. "They told LGBTQ+ people that we were criminals in our own country. That message ends today."Lawyer Anand Ramlogan SC, representing Jones, said the judgement was a "landmark victory for gay rights, equal dignity and respect for private and family life in Trinidad and Tobago."

Trinidad ⁠and Tobago’s law criminalising ⁠consensual sexual relations between ⁠male same-sex couples was overturned by a London court on Tuesday, after a legal challenge by a gay man who said the law breached his human rights.

Jason Jones challenged the Caribbean nation’s ‌Sexual Offences Act – which made “buggery” and “gross indecency” illegal – as breaching his fundamental rights under the country’s constitution.

London’s Privy Council, the final court of appeal for Trinidad and Tobago, ruled in Jones’ favour, saying it was unconstitutional for the law to “criminalise private, consensual sexual relations between adults of the same ⁠sex”.

Jones, who was born in Trinidad and Tobago and now lives in Britain, ‌welcomed the ruling but added that it did not address wider issues of “human rights and equality for LGBTQ+ people which ‌have been denied using British colonial era laws across the Commonwealth ⁠and beyond”.

The office ⁠of Trinidad and Tobago’s Attorney General, which opposed Jones’ appeal, did not immediately respond to ‌a request for comment.

Tuesday’s ruling is the latest concerning LGBTQ rights in the Caribbean, where some nations ‌still have ‌laws forbidding intimacy between people of the same sex, a legacy of ‌British colonial-era statutes.

Jones had initially won his case at Trinidad and Tobago’s High ⁠Court in 2018, but that ruling was overturned, prompting Jones to go to ⁠the Privy Council, which ruled that Trinidad and Tobago’s law was unconstitutional.

Judge Philip Sales said as he announced the court’s ruling that “the ‌current understanding of the ‌fundamental individual right to respect for private and family life is that it protects such a core part of human identity as one’s sexual orientation”.

“Laws which seek to criminalise such activities cannot be justified,” Sales added.
